name: Kevin Chou
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Kabam (originally Watercooler) in 2006 at age 26, a VC-backed social gaming company that later sold for ~$800M-$1B.
early_history_summary: Chou grew up in Moorpark, CA, the only child of Taiwanese immigrants; his father, a defense engineer, was laid off when Chou was in high school, creating financial urgency. He graduated magna cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa from UC Berkeley Haas, worked briefly in investment banking at Deutsche Bank, then joined Canaan Partners as a junior VC before founding Kabam with three co-founders in 2006, incubated at Canaan's offices.
family_context_summary: Only child of Taiwanese immigrants; father was a defense engineer who was laid off when Chou was in high school, plunging the family into financial difficulty. Parents divorced. Chou attended UC Berkeley on financial aid.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a defense engineer; no evidence of parental domain expertise in gaming, tech, or consumer internet. Chou traded penny stocks with his father, providing some early financial literacy.
primary_early_advantage_tags: UC Berkeley Haas, Canaan Partners, Silicon Valley, Facebook platform wave, financial hardship
evidence_summary: Chou graduated from UC Berkeley Haas magna cum laude, then worked at Deutsche Bank and Canaan Partners before founding Kabam at age 26 in 2006, incubated at Canaan's offices with $250K seed funding. His VC network at Canaan provided critical early support, and the company rode the Facebook platform wave. Family financial hardship from his father's layoff and parents' divorce created urgency but no inherited platform. Kabam later grew to $400M+ annual revenue and sold for ~$800M-$1B in 2017.
starting_point: Born to Taiwanese immigrant parents in a middle-class suburb of Los Angeles; father was a defense engineer who was laid off when Chou was in high school, creating financial hardship and parents' divorce.
current_position: Co-founder and executive chairman of Gen.G esports; co-founder of Forte Labs, Rally, SuperLayer, and Bright Saver; serves on UC Berkeley Board of Trustees. Kabam exit generated nearly $1B in value.

trajectory.event: Co-founded Watercooler (later Kabam) with three co-founders, incubated at Canaan Partners with $250K seed funding.
Rebranded Watercooler as Kabam and launched Kingdoms of Camelot, which became a $250M franchise.
Named to Fortune's '40 under 40' list of the world's most influential young people in business.
Sold Kabam's studios to Netmarble, 21st Century Fox, and GAEA for ~$800M-$1B total; co-founded Gen.G esports and Forte Labs.
Forte raised at a multi-billion dollar valuation from a16z, SEA, Kora, and other major investors.
Co-founded Bright Saver, a nonprofit making solar energy accessible to renters and homeowners.

name: Aaron Harris

early_history_summary: Harris attended Harvard University and worked at Bridgewater Associates as a hedge fund analyst before founding Tutorspree (YC Winter 2011 batch) and later becoming a YC partner in October 2013.
evidence_summary: Harris attended Harvard University and worked at Bridgewater Associates before founding Tutorspree in 2011 at age 31. He became a YC partner in 2013 at age 33, funding over 1000 companies. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Benjamin Black
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 verified; Black co-authored the first EC2 proposal paper at Amazon in 2003, but his birth year is undocumented, making it impossible to confirm the milestone occurred by age 26. Based on career trajectory (Internap R&D before Amazon in 2002), he was likely in his late 20s at the time.
early_history_summary: Black worked at Internap's R&D team (awarded 3 patents in internet routing) before joining Amazon in 2002 as a network engineer hired by Chris Pinkham. In 2003, he and Pinkham co-authored a paper proposing standardized, automated Amazon infrastructure that mentioned selling virtual servers as a service, which became the genesis of EC2.
evidence_summary: Black co-authored the first EC2 proposal at Amazon in 2003 with Chris Pinkham, which Jeff Bezos approved and led to AWS. However, his birth year is undocumented, and his prior career at Internap (with 3 patents) suggests he was likely in his late 20s when the EC2 paper was written, making it impossible to confirm a milestone by age 26. The Wikipedia page for 'Benjamin Black' is a disambiguation page; the AWS engineer has no dedicated Wikipedia article.

name: Naomi Ceder
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Ceder earned a PhD in Classics (Latin and Ancient Greek) and was teaching at a private school before beginning to work with computers in 1995 and Python in 2001. Her prominence came as PSF chair (2017-2020), well after age 26.
early_history_summary: Ceder earned a PhD in Classics with a minor in Indo-European Linguistics, then taught Latin at a private school. She began tinkering with computers and open source software (Yggdrasil Linux) around 1995, started using Python in 2001 after attending Guido van Rossum's tutorial at Linux World, and became a leader in the Python community over the following decades.
evidence_summary: Ceder pursued a PhD in Classics and taught Latin before transitioning to computing in 1995 and Python in 2001. Her community leadership (PSF chair 2017-2020, author of The Quick Python Book) came decades after age 26. No material milestone by age 26 was found; her tech career began well into adulthood.

name: Kent Beck
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Beck completed his BS and MS in computer and information science at the University of Oregon by 1987 (age 26) and was beginning his career as a Smalltalk programmer at Tektronix. His major contributions — SUnit, Extreme Programming, JUnit, and the Agile Manifesto — all came after age 30.
early_history_summary: Beck attended the University of Oregon from 1979 to 1987, earning BS and MS degrees in computer and information science. He discovered design patterns as an undergraduate through Christopher Alexander's work and began collaborating with Ward Cunningham at Tektronix, but his landmark creations (SUnit, XP, JUnit, Agile Manifesto) came in the 1990s and 2000s.
family_context_summary: Beck's father, Doug Beck, wrote process control software in assembly language for 8-bit microprocessors, which influenced Kent's later ideas about incremental change in software.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father wrote process control software in assembly language for 8-bit microprocessors, providing early exposure to programming concepts and the idea of making changes in small steps.
evidence_summary: Beck earned BS and MS degrees from the University of Oregon by 1987 (age 26) and was starting his career as a Smalltalk programmer at Tektronix. His foundational work with Ward Cunningham on patterns was beginning but had not yet achieved material recognition. His major creations — SUnit, Extreme Programming (1999), JUnit, and the Agile Manifesto (2001) — all came after age 30. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Nick Begich III
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Begich earned a BBA from Baylor (1999) and an MBA from Indiana University (2002), then worked at Ford Motor Company's IT Leadership Program before founding FarShore Partners in May 2006 at approximately age 29.
early_history_summary: Begich earned a BBA in Entrepreneurship from Baylor University (1999) and an MBA in Information Technology from Indiana University Bloomington (2002). He was a multi-year Top Achiever in the Ford Motor Company IT Leadership Program before founding FarShore Partners, a global software development company, in 2006. He later co-founded Dashfire and was elected to the U.S. Congress from Alaska in 2022.
family_context_summary: Begich comes from a prominent Alaska political family; his grandfather was U.S. Representative Nick Begich Sr. and his uncle was U.S. Senator Mark Begich. Family from Podlapaca in Lika, Croatia.
parent_family_domain_summary: The Begich family has deep political connections in Alaska, but no documented evidence of parental technology or business domain expertise relevant to his software company founding.
evidence_summary: Begich earned a BBA from Baylor (1999) and MBA from Indiana University (2002), then worked at Ford's IT Leadership Program before founding FarShore Partners in May 2006 at approximately age 29. His political career (elected to U.S. Congress in 2022) came much later. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Steve Westly
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Westly was working in government and energy policy roles in his 20s (Capitol Hill, U.S. Department of Energy, California Public Utilities Commission). His tech career began at Netcom in 1994 (age 37) and eBay in 1997 (age 40).
early_history_summary: Westly began his career in Washington, D.C., working on Capitol Hill and at the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Conservation and Solar. He returned to California as special assistant to the President of the California Public Utilities Commission, where he published two books on energy and utilities. He later earned an MBA from Stanford and worked at Sprint before joining Netcom (1994), WhoWhere (1995), and eBay (1997) as an early senior executive.
evidence_summary: Westly worked in government and energy policy through his 20s and 30s before entering tech at Netcom (1994, age 37) and eBay (1997, age 40). He helped take eBay public in 1998 and later served as California State Controller (2003-2007). No material milestone by age 26 was found; his tech and political achievements came in his late 30s and beyond.

name: Jewel Burks Solomon
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Partpic in 2013 at age 23, a computer vision startup that raised over $2M in seed funding and was acquired by Amazon in 2016; by age 26 the company had secured funding and built groundbreaking parts-identification technology.
early_history_summary: Burks Solomon grew up working in her family's businesses (insurance agency, real estate, convenience stores, laundromat) from a young age in Nashville, TN. She studied business at Howard University, graduating in 2010, interned at Google (2009), then worked in Google Enterprise sales (2010-2012). After moving to Atlanta for family reasons, she worked at McMaster-Carr as a customer service manager, where she identified the industrial parts identification problem that led to co-founding Partpic with Jason Crain in 2013.
family_context_summary: Mother ran an insurance agency for 25 years; father managed real estate, convenience stores, and a laundromat; grandfather founded businesses in Mobile, Alabama in the 1960s. Burks Solomon worked in family businesses from a young age, gaining early entrepreneurial exposure.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were small business entrepreneurs across multiple ventures (insurance, real estate, retail), transferring general business and entrepreneurial fluency, though not in technology specifically.
primary_early_advantage_tags: family business background, Google experience, McMaster-Carr customer exposure, computer vision, diversity in tech, family illness catalyst
evidence_summary: Burks Solomon grew up working in her family's multiple small businesses in Nashville, giving her early entrepreneurial fluency. After graduating from Howard University (2010) and working at Google, family health issues drew her back to Atlanta where a customer service job at McMaster-Carr exposed her to the industrial parts identification problem. She co-founded Partpic at age 23 in 2013 with Jason Crain, raised $2M+ in seed funding, and sold to Amazon in 2016. Her domain insight came from direct customer exposure, and she rode the computer vision/AI wave.
starting_point: Born in Mobile, Alabama; grew up in Nashville, Tennessee in a family of small business entrepreneurs (mother ran an insurance agency, father managed real estate and convenience stores; grandfather founded businesses in the 1960s).
current_position: Managing partner at Collab Capital ($125M+ fund); former head of Google for Startups US; co-founded Partpic (acquired by Amazon 2016). Resides in Atlanta, GA.

trajectory.event: Interned at Google as a BOLD intern in Mountain View while still a student at Howard University.
Co-founded Partpic with Jason Crain, a computer vision startup for industrial parts identification, after discovering the problem at McMaster-Carr.
Sold Partpic to Amazon for an undisclosed sum; joined Amazon to integrate Partpic technology as Amazon PartFinder.
Became first head of Google for Startups US and co-founded Collab Capital, a venture fund focused on Black entrepreneurship.
Collab Capital launched its first $51M fund investing in 36 Black-led companies across the US.

name: Evan Sharp
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Sharp was studying architecture at Columbia University (2007-2009) and working as a freelance designer at age 26. He co-founded Pinterest in March 2010 at age 27-28, after the qualifying age.
early_history_summary: Sharp grew up in York, Pennsylvania, where both parents were park rangers. He taught himself to code on his father's Macintosh and spent high school creating icons and user interfaces. He earned a BA in history from the University of Chicago (2005), worked at City Hall and a software company in Chicago, then studied architecture at Columbia (2007-2009). He took a sabbatical to work at Facebook as a product designer before co-founding Pinterest with Ben Silbermann in 2010.
family_context_summary: Both parents were park rangers in York, Pennsylvania. His father was an enthusiastic computer hobbyist who owned a Macintosh, which Sharp used to teach himself coding as a child.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a computer hobbyist with a Macintosh, providing early exposure to computing and design tools, though not in a professional or industry capacity.
evidence_summary: Sharp grew up tinkering with his father's Macintosh and creating icons in high school. He studied history at the University of Chicago (2001-2005) and architecture at Columbia (2007-2009), with freelance design work and a stint at Facebook in between. He co-founded Pinterest in March 2010 at age 27-28, designing and coding the initial product and the Pinterest grid. No material milestone by age 26 was found; Pinterest launched after the qualifying age.

name: Peter Thiel
milestone_by_age_26: Founded The Stanford Review in 1987 at age 20, an independent student newspaper that became a lasting institution and a pipeline for Silicon Valley talent (the 'PayPal Mafia'); also graduated Stanford Law with a JD in 1992 at age 25 and published The Diversity Myth in 1995.
early_history_summary: Thiel was born in Frankfurt, Germany, and moved to the U.S. as an infant. His father, a chemical engineer, moved the family frequently (including to Namibia) before settling in the U.S. Thiel studied philosophy at Stanford University, where he co-founded The Stanford Review in 1987 as a sophomore to challenge campus political orthodoxy. He graduated with a BA in 1989 and a JD from Stanford Law in 1992, then worked as a securities lawyer and derivatives trader before co-founding PayPal in 1998.
family_context_summary: Born in Frankfurt, Germany to Klaus Friedrich Thiel (a chemical engineer) and Susanne Thiel. Family moved to the U.S. when Peter was one, then to South African-occupied Namibia, then back to the U.S. in 1977. Father worked for various mining companies, creating an itinerant upbringing.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a chemical engineer who worked for mining companies; no evidence of direct parental domain expertise in technology, finance, or entrepreneurship. The family's mobility suggests a professional but not wealthy background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Stanford University, Stanford Review, Silicon Valley, conservative/libertarian network, PayPal Mafia pipeline
evidence_summary: Thiel co-founded The Stanford Review in 1987 at age 20, creating a lasting institution that became a talent pipeline for Silicon Valley (the 'PayPal Mafia'). He leveraged Stanford's elite ecosystem to build a network of contributors who later joined him at PayPal and beyond. His father was a chemical engineer with an itinerant career; the family was professional but not wealthy. Thiel graduated from Stanford (BA 1989, JD 1992) and worked as a lawyer and derivatives trader before co-founding PayPal in 1998 at age 31. His Stanford network was the dominant early advantage.
starting_point: Born in Frankfurt, Germany to a chemical engineer father and homemaker mother; family immigrated to the U.S. when Thiel was one, lived in Ohio and Namibia before settling in California in 1977. Professional, middle-class upbringing with frequent relocations due to father's mining industry career.
current_position: Founder and partner at Founders Fund; chairman of Palantir Technologies; co-founder of PayPal, Palantir, and Founders Fund; net worth ~$27.5B as of December 2025. Resides in Los Angeles, CA.

trajectory.event: Co-founded The Stanford Review as a sophomore at Stanford University, creating a conservative/libertarian student newspaper that became a lasting institution and Silicon Valley talent pipeline.
Graduated from Stanford University with a BA in philosophy.
Graduated from Stanford Law School with a JD; subsequently worked as a clerk, securities lawyer, and derivatives trader at Credit Suisse.
Co-founded Confinity (later PayPal) with Max Levchin and Luke Nosek, serving as CEO.
Sold PayPal to eBay for $1.5 billion; PayPal Mafia alumni went on to found numerous major tech companies.
Became the first outside investor in Facebook with a $500,000 angel investment.
Co-founded Founders Fund, a venture capital firm that invested in SpaceX, LinkedIn, Airbnb, and other major tech companies.

name: Timothy W. Bickmore
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Bickmore earned his BSE in Computer Systems Engineering (1985) and MS in Computer Science (1986) from Arizona State University, then worked as a research scientist at the Lockheed Artificial Intelligence Center (1986-1990). His major contributions (relational agents, PhD from MIT Media Lab in 2003) came well after age 26.
early_history_summary: Bickmore earned his BSE (summa cum laude) and MS from Arizona State University in 1985 and 1986 respectively. He worked as a research scientist at Lockheed's AI Center (1986-1990), then as a project engineer at Aerojet (1990-1994) and consulting scientist at Fuji Xerox PARC (1995-1998) before joining the MIT Media Lab for his PhD (completed 2003), where he introduced the concept of relational agents.
evidence_summary: Bickmore earned his BSE and MS from Arizona State University by 1986 and worked as a research scientist at Lockheed's AI Center. His major academic contributions — the concept of relational agents and his PhD from the MIT Media Lab — came in 2003, well after age 26. No material milestone by age 26 was found; his early career was competent but not notably distinguished.

name: Nils Lahr
milestone_by_age_26: By age 23, Lahr had worked on the world's first streaming broadcast at CNNfn (1995-1996), created the first automated stock ticker for TV, developed streaming media solutions at VXtreme (acquired by Microsoft 1997), and became a founding member of Microsoft's streaming media division in 1996.
early_history_summary: Lahr started programming at age 16, writing object-oriented databases for the U.S. Geological Survey where his father was a research seismologist. He attended Menlo-Atherton High School and earned a BS in Computer Science from NYU Polytechnic. He worked at CNNfn as webmaster for the world's first streaming broadcast and built the first fully digital studio, then joined VXtreme (acquired by Microsoft 1997) before becoming a founding member of Microsoft's streaming media division in 1996 at age 23.
family_context_summary: Born in 1973 to John C. Lahr, a research seismologist at the U.S. Geological Survey (1971-2003), and Karen Ericson. Father's position at USGS gave Nils early access to computing resources, leading him to start programming at age 16 by writing OODBs for USGS.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a research seismologist at USGS for 32 years; while not in the same domain (streaming media), the father's scientific workplace provided Nils with early access to computing resources and an environment that valued technical work.
primary_early_advantage_tags: USGS programming, early computing access, streaming media pioneer, CNNfn, Silicon Valley, internet wave
evidence_summary: Lahr started programming at 16 by writing OODBs for the USGS, where his father was a research seismologist. By his early 20s, he was at CNNfn working on the world's first streaming broadcast and building the first fully digital studio. He then developed streaming solutions at VXtreme (acquired by Microsoft 1997) and became a founding member of Microsoft's streaming media division at age 23. His streaming media expertise was exceptionally scarce for the mid-1990s, and he rode the early internet/streaming wave. His father's USGS position provided early computing access but no direct domain transfer.
starting_point: Born in 1973 to John C. Lahr, a research seismologist at the U.S. Geological Survey, and Karen Ericson; grew up with early access to computing through his father's workplace at USGS, starting to program at age 16.
current_position: Founder and CEO of OrionsWave LLC and Lani Quantum Solutions; former CTO and partner of Microsoft's Live AI division (2020-2023); Emmy winner for streaming media architecture. Resides in Snoqualmie, WA.

trajectory.event: Started programming at age 16, writing object-oriented databases for the U.S. Geological Survey.
Worked at CNNfn as webmaster for the world's first streaming broadcast; built the first fully digital studio and created the first automated stock ticker for TV.
Joined VXtreme developing streaming media solutions, then became a founding member of Microsoft's streaming media division after VXtreme's acquisition.
Founded OrionsWave, a venture firm and incubator for streaming media and AI companies.
Co-founded Orions Systems (AI vision systems), which was acquired by Microsoft to enhance Dynamics 365 capabilities.
Completed tenure as CTO and partner of Microsoft's Live AI division, overseeing $5.44B in revenue and real-time AI efforts.
